questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: English speaking country

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Checked in at uni accomodation and the staff and volunteers here were very helpful with any questions

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The Information before arrival was a bit shaky, but everything became clear when i arrived

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Apparently there were a few options, but i was only allowed to apply for "Accommodation". I could not specify whether i wanted to stay in the Urban Community or the Residential Village. The RV is a lot of halls much closer to a danish dorm, while the UC is more independent living with private bathrooms and small private kitchens.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: If you were to stay in Mannix hall, everything would be catered. If you stayed in the Urban Community you had a small private kitchen. If you stayed in the Residential Village, you had a few different options depending on the hall. Personally, I stayed in Roberts Hall, which meant that we had one kitchen with 8 stoves shared my 190 people. This was awful and i would absolutely not recommend it to anyone.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Do not stay in the Residential Village, as everyone is around 18-21 years old and have never lived away from home before. Go to the Urban Community - I would personally have chosen South East Flats or Campbell Hall if I had the choice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I liked staying on campus, but my friends who stayed in the CBD (in the heart of Melbourne) also said they had a great time, but just didn't see us that much as there is quite a way from Clayton and the uni to Melbourne CBD

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I was contacted by the abroad coordinator from KU and from Monash with very clear instructions. My emails were answered the next day due to timezones, but if you were available in their working hours they would get back to you almost immediately.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Email

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very - I got all the units I wanted. I took to master's and two bachelor's units while enrolled as a Master's Student. I had to choose 4-6 master's units, send in my application, and then email them saying which units i did not want to take and thereby replace with the bachelor's units. It is not possible to choose both Bsc and Msc units in the first application, but they are very helpful via email.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed having more free time by taking 50/50 bsc and msc courses. If you really have a look at the handbook for the year when choosing courses, it is possible to place all your lectures over 2-3 days and thereby have a lot of time for trips during the semester!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: MA courses felt like they were BA level, and BA courses felt like they were 9th grade - gymnasium level. I had a lot of free time on my hands.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Ba courses equals 2 hours of lectures a week and MA courses equals 3 hours of lectures a week. This means that you have a lot of time for assignments and quizzes, of which there are a lot. Everything is assessed during the course, leading to me practically having no exams. In reality, my exchanged was from March-May and the rest of the time was spent travelling.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FSC5051 - Innovation consumer behaviour and food marketing
ATS1141 - Japanese introductory 1
ATS1873 - Introduction to international relations
FSC5080 - Food science and technology in practice

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: They were all fun, so I'd recommend them all. I do think it would have been fun to go for more aboriginal-minded courses to learn more about their history and culture! I also had some friends taking Happiness 101 and Mindfulness 201 which sounded like a lot of fun, but perhaps not so academic. I would highly recommend taking a language course, as i enjoyed the Japanese course very much.

Food DKK per month *

Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Bought a bike in order to go to the grocery store and not having to walk for 25 minutes each way. Around 1200DKK.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Visa + mandatory health insurance was super expensive: Visa: 8.900DKK + OSHC: 1.900DKK + Danish health insurance: 2.500DKK.
Rent was absurd for what was offered: 7.300DKK/month
Ticket home at the end of my exchange was super expensive because of the world situation: 11.000DKK
Plane ticket to Australia was fine: 6.400DKK

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Literally all any club you can imagine - sports and cultural. They charge a fee to join, and then every activity also costs money to join, but it was worth it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined the Outdoor club and the Boardriders club in order to get to do some hiking and surfing. These were very cool and i would highly recommend them. If you already have a sport you enjoy, then absolutely join that club, but if not, i'd recommend the Dodgeball club!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go explore Victoria! The on campus residential service has trips around VIC which i recommend. Furthermore, go to the 1000 steps, Werribee Gorge, Wilsons Prom, Healsville Sanctuary, and explore Melbourne City! Queen Victoria Market, Skydeck, St. Kilda Penguins!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: There are so many exchange students at Monash, so when you actually find Australians, try to befriend them :P

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The use of AI at universities is insane - that was my biggest cultural chock!! They use it for everything and it is accepted in all classes...

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness of everyone here!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go for the courses you think are most difficult - they are probably not that bad.
Stay on campus and make friends that you can go travel with.
Join 3+ clubs on campus!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be ready for a lot of confusion at the start - the IT and facilities are new, but weirdly out of order a lot.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends! I made so many good friends that i was able to travel with around the country and to New Zealand later.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The housing situation. Living with teenagers is not a vibe when you are 26...

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Have such a great time in Melbourne!!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
